pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Famous Dinosaur Species (ages 5–7): recognise and name well-known dinosaurs — Tyrannosaurus rex, Triceratops, Stegosaurus, and a long-necked giant (Brachiosaurus/Diplodocus) — and describe one signature feature of each.
• Standards — UK (DfE): no KS1 statutory dinosaur naming, but supports 'working scientifically' (identify and classify, describe features) and vocabulary building; a common, high-engagement enrichment context in EYFS/KS1.
• Standards — US (NGSS): no K–2 PE for named species; supports the observation/description practices that underpin later fossil work (3-LS4-1).
• Operational details — This is a NAMING + one-distinguishing-feature task, not classification: T. rex (huge head, tiny arms, sharp teeth), Triceratops (three horns + neck frill), Stegosaurus (back plates + tail spikes), long-neck giant (very long neck and tail, tiny head). Attach ONE memorable visible feature per species so name recall is anchored to a picture, and ensure the child can match a name to an image unaided. Use correct names but keep to four to avoid overload; pronounce clearly. Keep this separate from diet or grouping (later topics).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~5): names two or three dinosaurs from pictures. Tier B (~6): names four and gives a feature for at least two. Tier C (~7): matches all four names to pictures unaided and states each one's signature feature.
bestPractices: Anchor each name to ONE unmistakable visual feature (three horns, back plates, tiny arms, long neck) so recall is picture-cued.
Use consistent, clear silhouettes/profiles — young children identify dinosaurs by shape, so distinctive outlines aid recognition.
Introduce a small fixed set (four) and revisit repeatedly rather than flooding with many species.
Pair the name with the feature in speech every time ('Triceratops — three horns') to bind label to attribute.
Keep naming separate from diet/size/grouping so the cognitive load is just name–picture–feature.
keyRepresentations: Clear species profiles/silhouettes with the signature feature highlighted (horns, plates, arms, neck).
A 'feature spotlight' that circles the diagnostic part as the name is spoken.
Comparison line-up of the four so their shapes contrast.
commonMisconceptions: 'Any big/spiky dinosaur is a T. rex' — T. rex is one specific species with a huge head and tiny arms.
'Stegosaurus and other plated/spiked dinosaurs are the same' — back plates + tail spikes distinguish Stegosaurus.
'Long-necked dinosaurs are pterodactyls/other creatures' — the long-neck giants are sauropods, still dinosaurs.
'All these dinosaurs lived together at the same time' — they lived in different periods (covered later).
'The name describes its diet' — naming and diet are separate; a name like Triceratops means 'three-horned face', not what it ate.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, help children recognise and name four well-known dinosaurs — Tyrannosaurus rex, Triceratops, Stegosaurus, and a long-necked giant (Brachiosaurus/Diplodocus) — by anchoring each name to ONE unmistakable visible feature (big head + tiny arms; three horns + frill; back plates + tail spikes; very long neck + small head). This is a naming + single-feature task, kept separate from diet, size or grouping. The aim is picture-cued recall: the child can match name to image unaided and state each one's signature feature, naming from a visible clue rather than guessing.

activities.title: Meet the four — name and feature line-up
feedback: If the child points to the correct feature, confirm by naming it together: 'Yes — three horns, so it's Triceratops.'
If they pick the wrong dinosaur, place the two profiles side by side and contrast the stand-out features (long neck versus tiny arms + big head) before naming again.
Keep to just these four and revisit them repeatedly rather than adding more species.
activities.rationale: Binding each name to one unmistakable, picture-cued feature in speech every time reduces cognitive load to name–picture–feature and anchors recall to a distinctive shape. A clear fixed 2D profile with the diagnostic part highlighted is sufficient for four-species recognition at this age.
sourceClaims: Signature features of common species: Tyrannosaurus rex (large skull, short two-fingered arms), Triceratops (three horns and a neck frill), Stegosaurus (dorsal plates and tail spikes/thagomizer), Brachiosaurus/Diplodocus (very long neck and tail, small head).
learnerActions: Look at clear profiles or silhouettes of all four dinosaurs side by side.

For each one, hear its name spoken clearly while pointing to its one stand-out feature: 'Tyrannosaurus rex — huge head and tiny arms', 'Triceratops — three horns and a neck frill', 'Stegosaurus — back plates and tail spikes', 'Brachiosaurus — very long neck and small head'.
Say each name aloud paired with its feature after the adult.
In a later round, answer the lift-the-flap style question for each: 'What makes this one special?' before the feature is revealed again.
activities.intendedInsight: Each dinosaur name has a HOOK — a visible feature you can point to — so 'the one with three horns' reliably becomes Triceratops.

activities.title: Match the name to the shape (active recall game)
feedback: On a correct match, light up or point to the feature that confirms it ('plates — yes, Stegosaurus').
On an incorrect match, ask 'which feature tells you?' and compare the two candidate shapes before trying again.
Praise naming that cites a feature, not just a lucky guess.
activities.rationale: Matching names to silhouettes and a mystery-shape round build shape-based recognition and self-checking, reinforcing the name–feature link established in the line-up. This activity reinforces recall rather than first teaching it.
learnerActions: Drag or place each name label onto the matching dinosaur silhouette.
Try a 'mystery silhouette' round: identify a dinosaur from its outline alone, then name it.
When a match is correct, notice the signature feature being highlighted to confirm.
Say why: 'This is Stegosaurus because of the plates on its back.'
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising and naming from shape alone, and justifying with a feature, turns passive recognition into active recall.

activities.title: Which one is it? — check and name from a picture
feedback: Correct: the long-necked, four-legged one is Brachiosaurus (or Diplodocus) — the very long neck and small head are the giveaway; the two-legged one with the big head, sharp teeth and tiny arms is Tyrannosaurus rex.
If the child labels the long-necked one 'T. rex' too, contrast the features side by side — long neck versus tiny arms and big head — and re-match each name.
If they name without a reason, insist on the 'because': which feature tells you?
If they mis-assign a feature (e.g. thinks the back plates are wings, or that T. rex had big arms), re-anchor the species to its correct feature.
activities.rationale: Asking for the deciding feature discriminates a child who names every big dinosaur 'T. rex' from one who tells look-alikes apart by evidence. This can verify name–picture–feature recall, and a selection-only item does not require independent production; it checks rather than first builds recognition.
learnerActions: Answer 'Which one is Stegosaurus?' by choosing from pictures of the four.
Match each name to its described feature (e.g. 'three horns' → Triceratops).

Respond to the diagnostic prompt: shown a big four-legged dinosaur with a very long neck and small head (a shape cue), and a two-legged dinosaur with a huge head, sharp teeth and tiny arms, name each one AND say the feature that helped decide.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming rests on a visible feature, not a guess; the 'what feature helped you decide' step blocks pure name-guessing.

constraints: Keep to exactly four species to avoid overload; introduce them as a small fixed set and revisit repeatedly.
Keep naming separate from diet, size and grouping (later topics); pair only name + one visible feature, and do not infer feeding from neck length within this objective.
Use correct names and pronounce them clearly, but do not add more species.
Matching games and picture multiple-choice reinforce or verify recall; they are not the first point of teaching the name–feature link.

A clear 2D profile/silhouette is enough to name four species; a rotatable 3D model could let a child view a feature (e.g. plates) from several sides but is optional and adds interaction overhead — not required for this objective.

Recognition and matching tasks confirm the child can identify a name, but a multiple-choice selection alone does not require the child to independently recall or produce the name; include at least one prompt where the child names unaided and states the feature.

If both Brachiosaurus and Diplodocus are shown, distinguish them or use just one consistently, since they differ in proportions; otherwise treat 'the long-necked giant' as the target and accept either name.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the single source is marked verified:false. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and the pedagogical cognitive-load/binding principle is not itself source-backed.

The assessment's probe 'Why does a very long neck give you a clue about what that dinosaur ate?' links neck length to diet; the pedagogy explicitly keeps naming separate from diet. Treat this as a later-topic extension, not part of the naming objective; it is excluded from the core activities. The saved correctAnswer phrase 'long neck for reaching high leaves' carries the same diet inference and has been reduced to a visible-feature cue in the guidance.

The source claim lists both Brachiosaurus and Diplodocus as examples of the long-necked giant; treat 'the long-necked giant' as the target and accept either name. They differ in proportions, so if both are shown, distinguish them or use just one consistently.

The pedagogy misconceptions that long-necked sauropods are 'still dinosaurs' (unlike pterodactyls, which are not dinosaurs) and that these dinosaurs did not all live at the same time (different periods) are pedagogically useful background but beyond the four-species naming task; retained in context, not taught as core actions.

The in-role conversation format was rated a poor fit for this closed recognition task in the source; this is a catalog fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law, and is omitted rather than asserted as a universal limit.

probeDeeper: Triceratops — how many horns does it have, and where? What number is hidden in its name?
What were the plates along Stegosaurus's back for — flying, or something else?
Why does a very long neck give you a clue about what that dinosaur ate?
assess.correctAnswer: The long-necked, four-legged one is Brachiosaurus (or Diplodocus) — the long neck for reaching high leaves is the giveaway. The two-legged one with the big head, sharp teeth and tiny arms is Tyrannosaurus rex — the tiny arms and huge toothy head are its signature. Naming rests on a visible feature, not a guess.

errorPatterns.pattern: Every big or scary dinosaur is a T. rex.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast signature features side by side — long neck versus tiny arms and big head; match each name to its stand-out feature.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels the long-necked one T. rex as well.

errorPatterns.pattern: Names dinosaurs by guessing, without reference to any feature.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on the 'because' — which feature tells you? Build the habit of naming from evidence, not memory alone.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Offers names but can't say what feature led to them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mis-assigns a signature feature (e.g. thinks Stegosaurus's back plates are wings, or that T. rex had big arms).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor each species to its correct feature; discuss what the plates/arms were actually for.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attaches the wrong feature to a named species.

responseLevels.gap: Calls most dinosaurs by one name (e.g. all 'T. rex'); can't match a name to a distinctive feature.
responseLevels.full: Names at least four common species and identifies each by a distinctive feature, correctly telling look-alikes apart from the picture.
responseLevels.partial: Names some species and one feature, but muddles look-alikes or a signature feature.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I show you a big four-legged dinosaur with a very long neck reaching up high, and a two-legged dinosaur with a huge head, sharp teeth and tiny little arms. Which is which — name each one — and tell me the feature that helped you decide.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who calls every big dinosaur 'T. rex' can't use distinguishing features. A child who names by feature (long neck versus tiny arms) tells them apart. The tier-two 'what feature helped you decide' blocks pure name-guessing.
